title: Aamir Khan Tears Up About His Family, Shares Updates on ‘3 Idiots 2,’ ‘Andaz Apna Apna 2’ at Singapore Film Fest
full_text: Oct 22, 2026 7:22am PT Aamir Khan Tears Up About His Family, Shares Updates on ‘3 Idiots 2,’ ‘Andaz Apna Apna 2’ at Singapore Film Fest By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘The History Boys’ Returns to London West End After 20 Years, With Nicholas Hytner Back Directing Alan Bennett’s Play 6 hours ago ‘Mother Bhumi,’ ‘Rehana Maryam Noor’ and ‘The Tourist’ Producers Head to Indonesia’s JAFF Market for New Exchange Program 7 hours ago Netflix, Bengali Streamer Hoichoi Partner to Bring Series to Hindi, Tamil and Telugu Audiences 7 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Lim Aamir Khan broke down onstage at the Singapore International Film Festival on Thursday as he recalled realizing, during the COVID-19 lockdown, that three decades of nonstop work had cost him years with his family. The Bollywood superstar, who was handed the festival’s Screen Icon Award by Hong Kong director Peter Chan Ho-sun, also shed light on sequels to “3 Idiots” and “Andaz Apna Apna” during a wide-ranging in-conversation session moderated by Singapore comedian Rishi Budhrani. Related Stories 'Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl' Documentary Coming to Hulu and ESPN The emotional moment came late in the evening, when Khan was asked about the weakest point of his journey. He described himself as a lifelong workaholic who ate, slept and dreamed films, and said his family had always been understanding enough to leave him alone. Popular on Variety “When I was sitting in COVID and I was thinking, I said, you know, about 30 years have passed of my life. And it’s okay to work like a madman, completely obsessed with what you’re doing for one year, two years, five years. But if it goes on for 30 years, I mean, you’ve lost your relationships. Your kids have grown up, they’re adults now. So I felt a deep sense of loss,” Khan said. He paused, broke down, apologized and gathered himself as the audience broke into applause. An audience member handed him a box of tissues. Khan, wiping his tears away, said the experience pushed him to make a major change, and that for the last four years he has deliberately carved out time for his family and close friends. “I’m so glad that this thought occurred to me when I was 56 and not when I was 86, when it would be really too late to do anything about it,” he said. On a lighter note, Khan was asked whether a sequel to “3 Idiots,” the 2009 campus comedy directed by Rajkumar Hirani, is in the works. “Well, I’m not allowed to say a lot,” Khan said. “I think I can say this much, that yes, Raju is working on the script. In fact, hopefully once I’m back in the next couple of weeks, he’s going to narrate the final version to me. So, fingers crossed.” According to Budhrani, Khan had phoned Hirani in front of him the previous day to check whether he could share the news, and the filmmaker gave his blessing – though Hirani didn’t pick up the first time, as Khan had changed his number. Khan said he had shut his phone a few weeks earlier and is now off all apps, having found that scrolling could swallow three hours at a stretch. With many fans having shouted out their love for Rajkumar Santoshi’s 1994 cult comedy “Andaz Apna Apna,” Khan was asked whether a sequel is on the cards. “Well, I know that Raj Santoshi is working on something,” he said. “So let’s see what happens.” Asked if there was anything more, he replied: “Yeah, that’s all.” In the same answer about his weakest moments, Khan recounted an earlier low point from the start of his career. After his 1988 debut “Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak” became a hit, he signed nine films within six months, reasoning that if established stars could juggle dozens of projects, he could handle 10. Once shooting began, he realized his mistake and would come home and weep to his then-wife Reena. The films then flopped one after another, and he was branded a “one-film wonder.” “At that time, mentally and emotionally, I felt like I’m in quicksand. I’m sinking slowly, and the more I’m struggling to get out, the deeper I’m going,” Khan said. At that point, Mahesh Bhatt, then riding high on “Saaransh,” “Arth” and “Naam,” offered him a film. Khan had vowed to commit only when he loved the script, the director and the producer, and he didn’t like the script. After a sleepless night, he turned Bhatt down. “If I had compromised with that and I had been practical, and I had, you know, said, ‘Yes, sir, I’m doing the film,’ I think my entire career would have been a series of compromises,” he said. They would go on to work together in “Dil Hai Ke Manta Nahin” and “Hum Hain Rahi Pyar Ke.” Accepting the Screen Icon Award, Khan thanked the festival and said that having Chan present it made the moment special. “Filmmaking is a collective art form, and a lot of people contribute to each other’s work,” he said. Asked why his films have resonated in China, Khan said “3 Idiots” took off there and across the wider region east of India after young viewers began passing it around, prompting them to seek out his other work. “I mean, it’s the truth. For me, my popularity in China is thanks to piracy,” he said, while stressing that he is not an advocate of it. He attributed the deeper connection to what he called a shared “emotional key” between Indian and Chinese audiences, recalling that watching “Dangal” in a Chinese theater felt like watching it in India. Khan also revealed that he holds 50 to 60 test screenings of 25 people each for his films, and that the first test screening of “Taare Zameen Par” was a disaster. For smaller films whose budgets can’t absorb his usual fee, he said he skips the fee and takes a back end instead, so the producer is protected if the film doesn’t work. On artificial intelligence, Khan said he views it as another filmmaking tool, much like VFX, and pointed to a castle set that would once have required 200 carpenters to build. “My common sense is telling me that in the short term, for sure, people are going to lose jobs,” he said. Khan, who last attended the festival nine years ago with “Secret Superstar,” also has a 25th anniversary screening of “Lagaan,” his first film as producer, lined up at the festival on Friday. title: JJ Watt Named Lead Analyst For ‘NFL On CBS’
full_text: Skip to main content By Jill Goldsmith Jill Goldsmith Co-Business Editor More Stories By Jill Comcast Q3: Record-Breaking ‘The Odyssey’, Profitable Peacock Fuel NBCU Spinoff Momentum Netflix Jitters: Valid Concerns Or Market Overreaction? – “One Breakout Hit Could Shift Sentiment” Ted Sarandos Insists Netflix “Strategy Is Unchanged” As Execs Are Pressed About Growth View All October 22, 2026 7:20am Add us as a Google Preferred Source JJ Watt CBS CBS Sports announcer JJ Watt has been named lead analyst for the NFL ON CBS in a new multi-year agreement. The announcement made today by David Berson, Chairman, Global Sports Group, Skydance, calls for Watt to continue to call the network’s top games alongside Jim Nantz and Tracy Wolfson as CBS Sports’ lead NFL announce team, including next season when they call Super Bowl LXII in Atlanta. “I’ve had a front-row seat to JJ’s growth as a top-tier broadcaster, watching him tackle this role just like he did his hall-of-fame playing career,” said Berson. “He’s insightful, entertaining, passionate, meticulous in his preparation, and the ultimate teammate. He has a unique ability to see things and communicate to fans of all levels. We are thrilled to have him leading our NFL coverage.” Related Stories Sports CBS Sports Chief David Berson To Expand Portfolio As TNT Sports Chief Luis Silberwasser Exits Sports Tony Romo And CBS Sports Part Ways After His Drunk-Driving Arrest “I am incredibly honored and grateful to have the opportunity to represent CBS Sports and all of the fantastic people who make this place so special,” said Watt. “From the brotherhood of THE NFL TODAY to my crews calling games, I couldn’t ask for better teammates alongside me on this television journey. I am thankful to David Berson for his leadership, vision and trust. I love this job and can’t wait to see you Sunday with Jim and Tracy and many more Sundays to come!” Watch on Deadline Watt’s title comes after CBS Sports and Tony Romo parted ways earlier this month. Romo, a four-time Pro Bowl quarterback with the Dallas Cowboys, was arrested in a traffic stop in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, on July 23, and charged with operating while intoxicated. He pleaded no contest and the network initially put him on leave before severing ties. Watt joined CBS Sports in 2023 as a studio analyst on The NFL Today . Last season, Watt moved to the booth to call games with Ian Eagle and Evan Washburn. At the start of the 2026 season, he began calling games with the Network’s lead team, working with Nantz and Wolfson. Watt was a three-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and was honored as the 2017 Walter Payton NFL Man of the Year. He was inducted into the Houston Texans Ring of Honor in 2023. Drafted by Houston in the first round of the 2011 NFL Draft out of Wisconsin (No. 11 overall), Watt played 12 NFL seasons with the Texans (2011-20) and Arizona Cardinals (2021-22). A five-time NFL First-Team All Pro and five-time Pro Bowl selection, he is the only player in NFL history to record multiple seasons with at least 20 sacks and finished his career with 114.5 sacks. She posted on X, “After nine wonderful years at CNN, I’ve decided to leave for an opportunity that I couldn’t pass up. title: Brian Selznick’s Rome-Set Queer YA Romance ‘Run Away With Me’ Set For Feature Adaptation With Gianni Nunnari Producing
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman , Diana Lodderhose October 22, 2026 7:17am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Brian Selznick, 'Run Away with Me' and Gianni Nunnari Getty Images EXCLUSIVE : Hollywood vet and Italian native Gianni Nunnari , producer on movies including the 300 franchise , Immortals , and From Dusk Til Dawn , is bringing Brian Selznick ’s ( The Invention of Hugo Cabret ) young adult novel Run Away With Me to the screen, with Selznick adapting his own novel. Rome-born Nunnari, an exec producer on The Departed and Se7en , will produce through his Hollywood Gang Productions banner, with executive producer set as Deborah Belford de Furia. Published by Scholastic in 2025, Run Away With Me marked Selznick’s first novel written specifically for a young adult audience. Set in Rome in the 1980s, the queer coming-of-age romance follows Danny, a 16-year-old American spending the summer in Italy, whose life is transformed when he meets Angelo, a mysterious Italian boy. The novel blends more than 100 pages of Selznick’s signature illustrations with prose. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Hollywood Vet Gianni Nunnari & 'Magazine Dreams' Producer Simon Horsman Launch Film & TV Label Euro Gang With Footprints In London, Rome, Madrid & LA; Company Inks Deal With Warner Music Group For Scripted Slate News ESPN Original Series To Depict Formation Of Premier Lacrosse League Selznick is the Caldecott Medal-winning author and illustrator of The Invention of Hugo Cabret , which was adapted by Martin Scorsese into the five-time Academy Award-winning film Hugo . His novel Wonderstruck was adapted into the Todd Haynes-directed feature starring Julianne Moore, with Selznick writing the screenplay. His other works include The Marvels , Kaleidoscope and Big Tree , the latter originating from an idea developed with Steven Spielberg. Nunnari is expected to draw on his longstanding relationships in Hollywood and the European production community to mount the film on location in Rome. He most recently exec-produced Roland Emmerich’s swords and sandals epic Those About To Die in the city. James Canellos and Michael Ritter will also executive produce. The synopsis continues: “What begins as a chance encounter develops into an intense first love as Danny and Angelo explore the Eternal City together, uncovering stories hidden within its streets, monuments and ruins. Their romance is echoed by other love stories spanning the 17th century, 19th century and 1940s, revealing a history of queer love that has endured even when those relationships were forced into secrecy or erased from the historical record. As the boys grow closer, Angelo’s own secrets begin to emerge, forcing Danny to confront the possibility that their relationship, and the seemingly timeless Roman summer surrounding them, cannot last forever.” “ Run Away With Me is a universal story of love in the Eternal City, set in the 1980s, when I was falling in love with love and with Rome itself,” said Nunnari. “For me, bringing Brian’s story to the screen feels very personal.” Selznick added: “I’m thrilled my book is being brought to life by such an extraordinary team. We’re all eager to tell a story that affirms the importance of love, a message that feels more urgent now than ever.” Executive producer de Furia commented: “ Run Away With Me and Hollywood Gang may seem like an unlikely pairing, but they are a perfect combination. I’ve worked with Gianni for years and have seen firsthand his passion for storytelling, history, love, and Rome, while Brian is one of the most extraordinary creative minds working today and someone I’ve been lucky to know for decades. Run Away With Me pulses with the electricity of first love and the discovery that our own love stories belong to a history much larger than ourselves. And, of course, the Eternal City plays a starring role. Don’t we all want to fall in love in Rome?” Selznick is represented by CAA. title: Comcast Plans Major Layoffs as It Preps for NBCU Spin-Off, Sees $1 Billion-Plus Restructuring Charge in Q4
full_text: Oct 22, 2026 7:10am PT Comcast Plans Major Layoffs as It Preps for NBCU Spin-Off, Sees $1 Billion-Plus Restructuring Charge in Q4 By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Comcast Plans Major Layoffs as It Preps for NBCU Spin-Off, Sees $1 Billion-Plus Restructuring Charge in Q4 17 minutes ago Spotify Hums Along in Q3, Reaching 306 Million Paid Subscribers: ‘There Is More Runway Ahead’ 4 hours ago Will Elon Musk Help the Ellisons Pay Down Skydance’s Massive Debt? John Malone Predicts Tech Mogul’s SpaceX Could Invest up to $10 Billion Into Media Company 21 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images for Comcast Comcast is gearing up for significant job cuts in its cable and telecom business in the coming weeks, as the media conglomerate restructures ahead the expected spin-off of NBCUniversal in 2027. On the company’s third-quarter 2026 earning call, CFO Jason Armstrong said Comcast expects to take a restructuring charge of more than $1 billion in Q4. “We expect to have a significant charge in the fourth quarter related mostly to our transformation efforts, and I would quantify that at over $1 billion,” he told analysts. Related Stories 'Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl' Documentary Coming to Hulu and ESPN The scope of Comcast’s layoffs is yet to be determined, with individual teams currently assessing what the impact will be, according to two sources familiar with the situation. For now, the layoffs are expected to affect the Comcast Cable side of the business, not NBCU divisions. Popular on Variety Armstrong said the restructuring “is to get ahead of cost actions that will facilitate sort of a fast start into 2027” and are aimed at “strengthening our competitive position.” He continued: “We don’t look at it as a cost-cutting exercise. This is the ability to simplify in order to move faster, to be more nimble in decision-making, and I think really create capacity, you know, to invest for growth.” Part of Comcast’s growth initiatives involve stepping up its push into wireless services and business services. For the third quarter, revenue in Comcast’s connectivity and platforms business fell 2.7% to $19.66 billion, as it saw continued net losses of broadband and cable TV subscribers. Revenue from NBCU’s TV, film and theme parks operations rose 6.5% to $10.54 billion. Comcast in June announced that it will spin off NBCUniversal (together with Sky) in a tax-free transaction expected to be completed in mid-2027. Execs on the Q3 call reiterated that the spin-off timeline remains on track. The plans for the NBCU spin come after the separation of its cable networks (excluding Bravo) and other businesses into Versant Media, which closed in January of this year. As of Dec. 31, 2025, Comcast has about 179,000 employees. Comcast’s plans to cut jobs in cable TV, broadband and wireless segments were reported Wednesday by Bloomberg. title: ESPN Original Series To Depict Formation Of Premier Lacrosse League
full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Meta Tops Q3 Revenue Estimates, But Earnings Hit By Teen Lawsuit Settlement; Stock Split Creates Class C Shares John Malone Says Trump Administration Told Netflix They Had “No Chance” Of Getting Regulatory Greenlight For Merger With Warner Bros. Discovery Elon Musk & Larry Ellison Will Join Forces To Boost Both Starlink And Skydance, John Malone Predicts View All October 22, 2026 7:08am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Mike and Paul Rabil, brothers and co-founders of the Premier Lacrosse League Courtesy of ESPN Originals EXCLUSIVE: A five-part ESPN docuseries whose producers include Oscar nominee and multiple Emmy winner Matthew Heineman ( Cartel Land ) will chronicle the formation of the Premier Lacrosse League. At the center of the original series, titled The Big Leagues , will be brothers and PLL co-founders Mike and Paul Rabil . The project extends a close relationship between the league and ESPN, following a deal giving the Disney subsidiary a stake in the PLL along with media rights. The PLL championship game aired last month on ABC. Beyond the effort to create the league itself, the series will detail the brothers’ push to make lacrosse a major sport, with the rollout of the series timed to the runup to the 2028 Summer Olympics. Lacrosse will be an official event at the L.A. Games. Related Stories Sports 'Monday Night' Friction? ESPN NFL Broadcasters Joe Buck & Troy Aikman Have Noisy Start To Super Bowl Year Documentary Michael Jackson 1993 Super Bowl Halftime Show Documentary Set From Hulu & ESPN Paul Rabil, who segued to launching the league from a playing career that put him among the sport’s all-time greats at the college and pro level, is set to make his directing debut with The Big Leagues . Watch on Deadline Production is underway on the series, with premiere date and distribution plans still being finalized. The series is produced by ESPN Originals, Our Time Projects and Two Point Productions, with Heineman exec producing and Gene Gallerano serving as showrunner. “What drew us to this story is the opportunity to take viewers inside a side of professional sports they rarely get to see,” said Lindsay Rovegno, VP & Executive Producer, ESPN Originals. “ The Big Leagues is told through a unique voice that will capture the decisions, risks, and relationships that shape this young league with a bright but unpredictable future.” The series shows how Paul Rabil stepped aside as a player to team with his brother, who has been a serial entrepreneur. The pair navigated a range of financial, operational and cultural challenges of growing the sport of pro lacrosse, putting their fraternal and business relationship to the test. Heineman describes the series as “part American dream story, part family story, part sports story,” saying it “hits on deep, universal themes” and is “big in scope but deeply personal.” “This is a story about betting on something you believe in,” Paul Rabil said. “Mike and I set out to give players the league they deserved, and we’ve learned a lot the hard way. title: John Anderson Dies: Country Singer Of Hits ‘Wild And Blue’ & ‘Swingin” Was 71
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘860’ Broadway Review: Billy Crystal Remembers The Stuff Of Life And Loss Tom Cruise To Receive 52nd AFI Life Achievement Award Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Billy Crystal, Bradley Whitford Prove Strong Ticket Draws – Broadway Box Office View All October 22, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source John Anderson (2011) Rick Diamond/Getty Images for BMI John Anderson , one of the “New Traditionalist” country singers of the 1970s who broke into the mainstream with chart-topping hits like “Wild and Blue”, “Swingin'” and “Black Sheep”, died Wednesday, October 21, at his home in Smithville, Tennessee. He was 71. His death was announced by family on social media. A cause of death was not disclosed, but The LA Times reports that the singer died in his sleep. The family statement on Anderson’s Instagram page reads, “It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and best friend. To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely, and made every ordinary moment feel special. We are completely heartbroken.” Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries Obituaries Freddie Jackson Dies: R&B Hitmaker Behind “Rock Me Tonight”, “You Are My Lady” & Many More Was 70 The statement continues, “His music will live on, but for us, his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave his family and the memories we will carry with us forever.” Born December 13, 1954 in Apopka, Florida, Anderson moved to Nashville after high school, at first performing as a country duo with his sister before finding some success as a solo singer in the back-to-the-roots “New Traditionalist” movement alongside George Strait, Ricky Skaggs and Waylon Jennings, among others. Anderson, even while maintaining the hard-country, keening vocal style of his traditionalist roots, began a move into mainstream country success in the early 1980s with his rocking, uptempo hit “Swingin'” and, with a nod to the more traditionalist style, the fiddle-heavy title song from his 1982 album “Wild & Blue.” The album brought Anderson to the attention of the wider country radio audience, and earned a slew of Country Music Association award nominations, with “Swingin'” named Single of the Year and Anderson winning the Horizon Award for new artists. The ’90s brought continued success, including with the chart-topping singles “Straight Tequila Night” and “Money in the Bank,” and popular albums including Seminole Wind and Solid Ground . He continued recording well into the 2000s, but with more modest results. His final albums Goldmine and Years were released in 2015 and 2020, respectively. Anderson was inducted to the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame on October 5, 2014, and the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2024. Following Anderson’s death, country star and former The Voice coach Blake Shelton paid tribute on Instagram, writing, “There is too much for me to say about @johnanderson in just a statement. I am sick and I am stunned. But I am a very lucky man. I got the opportunity to find out that my hero wasn’t just the guy I hoped he’d be. He was so much more than that. John was my friend. I got to see him last Sunday and I don’t even know why but I told him I loved him. That is what fills my heart in this moment. My love and prayers go out to John’s family. This one really hurts.” Anderson is survived by his wife of more than 40 years, Jamie, and daughters Alexa Kate and Brionna Cheri. title: Chuck Lorre Talks David Ellison Optimism, Scientology and the Perks (Really!) of Working for Roseanne Barr
full_text: × Skip to main content By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All October 22, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Chuck Lorre Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images If scathing anecdotes from some of the most popular TV comedies of the last four decades are your thing, perhaps you’ve noticed that Chuck Lorre released a memoir. The showrunner behind Dharma and Greg, Two and a Half Men, The Big Bang Theory, Mom, Young Sheldon and many, many, many other series released Sitcom on Oct. 13. The book include Lorre’s take on Charlie Sheen ’s Two and a Half Men meltdown, a few other sitcom stars who pushed him to the edge (Brett Butler and Cybill Shepherd) and the one who did so while also helping his career ( Roseanne Barr). Related Stories Business David Ellison (Again) Says He Plans to Combine HBO Max and Paramount+ Movies David Ellison Says Skydance Will Make Original Swings Like 'Sinners' Naturally, reviving some of these fraught narratives seem to have irked some mentioned in the book. 20th Century curiosity Tom Arnold shot back at Lorre’s claim that Arnold demanded writers add his name to scripts when he was producing then-wife Roseanne Barr’s hit series. Arnold expressed his displeasure with the accusation on X and then called Lorre “a terrible human, an angry dry drunk who lies every time he opens his mouth.” Speaking to THR days later , Barr agreed with her ex-husband’s claim on writing credits — though not the character assassination. But as I learn over a phone call with Lorre, the super-producer does not seem interested in any more back-and-forth with former colleagues now that everything is on the page. (Those who take issue with any of his recollections, he suggests towards the end of Sitcom, can “write your own book.”) Fully prepared that this book would be full of shit talking, I feared there’d be some damning story about Christine Baranski , who co-starred in the apparently quite problematic Cybill . Thanks for not bursting my bubble. Oh my god. Christine Baranski is one of the great joys of my life — to have been able to work with her, not just on that show, but on The Big Bang Theory . Among the more surprising threads in the book is that, internally at CBS, she was referred to as “the death of comedy” during casting — as were Jon Cryer and Melissa McCarthy. Did these executives ever express any contrition when proven wrong? No. Listen, the big picture is that they’re extraordinarily good at casting dramas, but casting comedies was not their strong suit. You also have to acknowledge that CBS gave me a shot to do a show about quantum physicists. Yes, we disagreed on casting, but it’d be foolish to overlook how many opportunities I had with that company to figure it out and do it right. If a prophet came to you in 1992, the year you were fired from Roseanne , and said that you’d still be publicly battling over the behind the scenes drama of that show 34 years later… how would you have reacted? I don’t know how to answer that. It was a singular, extraordinary opportunity to be on that show. While it was difficult, I also benefited from it. I don’t think anybody who worked there didn’t come out a better writer for having been there. It might have crushed their soul in the process, but we all became better. And that’s because Roseanne insisted on honest, truthful storytelling about this family. She would not suffer any glib sitcom bullshit. You write about your decade in Scientology, sometimes critically and mockingly. In the past, that institution would really go after that kind of criticism. Did you have any discussions about the potential ramifications about how to write about your experience? Because people are rarely this candid about Scientology. The whole book is an effort to tell the truth of my experience and my journey to where I am right now. But at the same time, it was important for me to put in the book that there were benefits regarding that 10-year bubble that I was in. It’d be ridiculous to ignore the fact that for every mistake that I made and every poor choice that I made… surviving it, you can take a step back and go, “Well, here’s what I got from that.” And I made a point of putting that in the book that it’s not all negative. It’s not all just trash talking this organization. I did benefit in some ways that it would be disingenuous to ignore. Have you heard from anyone in that camp? No. I don’t think it’s worth it. I don’t think anybody gives a crap. You talk about a lot of people in here. Who got a heads up? I sent the pages about Charlie [Sheen] to Charlie and he signed off on it. And I ran everything past the ex-wives. I wanted to be careful to not hurt people. There are some passing jokes in the book about Warner Brothers’ many owners since you started there, but one could argue that you’re not just an employee. On the TV side, you’re responsible for a great deal of the studio’s success in the 21st century and arguably a factor in its value. Do you feel a personal stake as it changes hands again? I just know. I’ve been there now going on 28 years. I went in 1999 and they were going through the AOL mistake. But I’ve been the beneficiary and a lot of support from that company, starting with Peter Roth, who was immensely supportive. People tend to speak very kindly about Peter Roth. He loves television. He loves storytelling. He loves to laugh. That’s not always the case with executives. Generally, they’re running scared and they’re trying to figure out how to survive the job. Peter actually loved the job and he loved comedy. He was the one who offered me a job at Fox and that led to Dharma and Greg. He went to Warner Brothers and said, “No, come here.” So I followed him, because there’s an intangible quality that I’ve always gone after — which was to work with people that love what we do. That it’s not just creating content. And I have to say that [Skydance CEO] David Ellison made that very clear to me when I met him. He doesn’t like creating content. He wants to make stories and entertain. And that speaks to me. The idea that it’s content is depressing. “ Content” is a pretty gross term. It’s loathsome. I assume this meeting with David Ellison was quite recent. Maybe a month ago? But when I hear someone in that position say, “I’m not in the content business, I’m in the storytelling business,” that’s meaningful. That’s really meaningful because that’s what I try to do. I keep my job really simple. My job is to make people laugh. It appears to be memoir season for Hollywood’s great white men: Ari Emanuel’s book, the authorized Larry David biography , Bob Iger is releasing another memoir. Is something in the air? I don’t know. ( Laughs ) Serendipity? This was a two-year project for me and I’m glad it’s done. I really am. As I was writing, I was hoping that the book can cause laughter. Otherwise, what’s the point? I’m not in the education business. I’m not in the morality business. I’ve been in the comedy business for a long time and if I’m going to write a book, hopefully it causes laughter, otherwise the book fails. How did you find the experience of recording the audiobook? I was told that it’s difficult. “How tough can it be?” It’s actually really hard because you want to perform the book. You want to make sure that the jokes land and that the stories unfold and that it’s an entirely different experience. I wrote the book to be read, not to be listened to, but audiobooks are a big deal. I actually hadn’t considered it until the book was in, really. I did the very best I could. But you’re a writer of dialogue. Your writing, historically, are spoken. Would you have considered someone else narrating this? You would have had to showrun the recording. There was no chance I was going to let anybody read this. It made no sense to me to have someone read the story of my life. Two stories from your personal life really stood out to me. First, the coincidence of buying a guitar at a bar saved your life. I won’t spoil how. Second, an ex-girlfriend prevented you from having to spend your life with a colostomy bag by helping you change your diet. In recalling these strokes of fortune, did you have any grand realizations? I have a lot of gratitude. I’ve had angels cross my path over and over again. It became very clear in writing this book how lucky I’ve been. Because of the certain people who came along at just the right time to rescue me — sometimes from myself. Are you keeping as busy as usual? Stuart Fails to Save the Universe , Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage , Leanne Morgan’s show… I still go to work every day and try and cause laughter somehow. That’s not a bad gig, right? If you write another book in 20 years… Twenty years!? ( Laughs .) If you write another book in 20 years and reveal that Leanne Morgan ran a really toxic set, it’ll really bum me out. Leanne Morgan is a magnificent human being and that is not hyperbole. Somebody who’s a successful standup comedian, not everybody can make it acting. It’s a difficult transition. And she’s done that, and it’s a very happy set because she sets the tone. That’s Leanne’s nature. THR

title: Ben Silverman Still Doesn’t Want a Job — But He’s Busier Than Ever
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All October 22, 2026 6:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ben Silverman Valerie Macon / AFP via Getty Images Ben Silverman has been producing TV since he was 30. Twenty-six years later, the man does not lack for pep. He’s naturally a vibes guy, though the multiple double lattes probably help. On a Monday in late August, Silverman met The Hollywood Reporter at a coffeehouse opposite Manhattan’s Bryant Park to check in on Propagate Content — Silverman’s and his former assistant Howard T. Owens’ production company — but instead golf took over the chat. The Propagate chairman and co-CEO carries an 8.1 handicap and memberships at the ultra-exclusive Riviera and Hillcrest country clubs. As of late, Silverman’s hobby has informed his profession: Propagate has revived the Skins Game at Amazon, is developing an untitled Anthony Kim documentary and will premiere season two of the scripted Owen Wilson golf comedy Stick on Apple TV on Nov. 4. Meyer Silverman (a plus-2 handicap), Ben’s son and the top high school freshman earlier this month in the Colorado Class 3A Boys Golf State Championships, has already eclipsed Dad’s golf game. It’s kind of exactly how Ben built on his own parents’ creative careers. His father, Stanley Silverman, is a composer who has arranged music for Sting and Paul Simon; his mother, Mary (Delson) Silverman,was an opera singer, and his stepmother a violinist. “I kind of grew up in the arts but always seeing that it was a tough life,” Silverman recalls. “I had maggots in my cereal growing up. My dad, when he got divorced from my stepmom, had to move in with me and my mom.” Propagate Content’s Howard T. Owens and Ben Silverman along with Kenya Barris at the ‘Jerry West: The Logo’ premiere at The Culver Theater on April 13, 2026 in Culver City. Phillip Faraone/Getty Images for Prime Video An artist’s upbringing birthed a builder of others’ visions. As the youngest-ever division head at William Morris, Silverman saw the opportunity to repackage overseas formats for U.S. audiences. “That was a quiet business that had a couple of hustling, Willy Loman-type players in it — but otherwise was not a real business,” Silverman says. “I really led the charge in that.” From London, Silverman adapted Queer as Folk for Showtime and later Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? for ABC. Millionaire handed Silverman his Hollywood “I made it” moment. Massive TV ratings brought in phone calls from Disney chief Michael Eisner — “Thanks! What else you got?” — and NBC CEO Bob Wright: “Why didn’t I get Millionaire ?” (He passed on it but soon would buy The Weakest Link from Silverman.) “I’m like, ‘Oh my God, my life just changed,’ ” Silverman recounts. With the backing of Barry Diller, a 29-year-old Silverman left the agency to start Reveille Productions, which brought America The Office and Silverman his “I’ve really made it” moment. “My dad and I are sitting together on an airline… and 95 percent of the plane had chosen to watch The Office ,” Silverman says. “The entire plane was laughing.” “’Oh my gosh,’” he recalls thinking. “’My family’s life just changed.’” At 36, Silverman sold Reveille to the Murdochs for $125 million (who would flip it for seven times that, he says) and became co-chair of NBC Entertainment in 2007. It was the first job Silverman had that didn’t really suit him. The problem was the suit. He lasted two years. The Hollywood Reporter ‘s July 28, 2009 front page story on Silverman’s NBC exit. The Hollywood Reporter “I walked in [Jeff Zucker’s] office and said, “Jeff, this job gives me a stomachache. I do not like it. I feel like a sports car in a parking lot of Tauruses. I don’t enjoy this,”’ Silverman remembers. “’I feel like I’m managing up and managing down without getting to pursue the things I care about. I cannot do this anymore.’” He and Diller next launched Electus, which is now Propagate. Silverman says he won’t join the corporate ranks again. “I get the calls every couple of years, and I’m like, ‘Wait, that sounds like a job. I don’t want a job!’” Silverman says. “I just love being in culture,” he adds. And his own banner now has an undeniably large portfolio of projects — Netflix’s Untold , the CNN doc I’m Chevy Chase and You’re Not , Hulu’s The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives , Amazon’s Jerry West: The Logo , Food Network’s Chopped and scripted fare like The Paper (Peacock) and the upcoming Protective Custody (Apple TV) comedy series starring Ben Stiller and Benicio Del Toro — but Propagate is still seeking its first true society-shaker. That could come as early as November, when its Sam Bankman-Fried doc series The Boy Who Stole Billions? premieres on Amazon. Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM, approvingly screened it a few weeks ago. Hopkins credits Silverman’s “diverse set of relationships” and the “ability to work across a number of dimensions and genres” for his success. “And then he delivers,” Hopkins adds. “We’re a hit-driven business — not everything that every producer does is going to knock it out of the park — but [Silverman has] a really good track record.” Also in the Propagate pipeline is an untitled Mookie Betts scripted comedy from Ramy Youssef and Josh Rabinowitz in development for Apple TV, with an Entourage -like setup for the Dodgers’ star shortstop. (Betts will not personally play himself in the Vincent Chase-role.) The firm is additionally developing a scripted series with Jenny Bicks ( Sex and the City ) and another with Friends co-creator Marta Kauffman; Silverman is in negotiations with Netflix for the latter. Ben Silverman, Liz Tuccillo, Abigail Spencer, Josh Charles, Annie Potts, Cree, Josh Segarra, Rodney Ferrell and Wattson attend an FYC screening and panel for Fox’s “Best Medicine” on the Fox Studio Lot in Los Angeles, California on May 5, 2026. Getty Images For Fox’s Tuesday night hit Best Medicine , an American take on ITV hit Doc Martin , Silverman returned to his roots as an importer of culture. It was wise to pitch it to the British CEO of an American media company. “We had a lunch where we talked about Doc Martin and our shared passion for the series and the possibility of Liz [Meriwether] being involved,” Wade says. “We were both huge fans of the original. Doc Martin was so comedic, and Martin Clunes was known for sitcoms when it launched, and I think Ben’s understanding of really why that show worked helped me and Michael (Thorn, Fox network president) make the decision to buy it.” Josh Charles, who plays the Doc Martin (Clunes) role here, says Silverman charmed the Sports Night and The Good Wife star aboard with one deep pull outside of the TV ecosystem. “When we first spoke on the phone about Best Medicine and were discussing the overall tone of the show, he mentioned an older, more-obscure film I love called Local Hero ,” Charles tells THR, referencing the 1983 British comedy-drama written and directed by Bill Forsyth. “I was surprised he knew of it and I thought it was a perfect example of what the tone of the show could be, and it was in that moment I knew I wanted to be part of it.” Charles adds, “That’s good producing as far as I’m concerned.” Ben Silverman on the set of Apple TV’s ‘Stick’ with golfer Max Homa. title: Egyptian Screenwriter Mariam Naoum on the Struggle for Arab Series to Find Buyers: ‘We’re Suffocating Inside’
full_text: Oct 22, 2026 6:40am PT Egyptian Screenwriter Mariam Naoum on the Struggle for Arab Series to Find Buyers: ‘We’re Suffocating Inside’ CineGouna Series head seeks to clear obstacles that hinder writing talent in the Arab world By Essie Assibu Plus Icon Essie Assibu Latest Sequel to Egyptian Hit ‘Sleepless Nights’ Eyes 2027 Shoot as New Details Revealed (EXCLUSIVE) 20 hours ago Sharjah Film Festival Expands Opportunities for Young Filmmakers: ‘There Is No Shortage of Talent’ 24 hours ago Sharjah Film Festival Unveils Lineup With ‘Gohan,’ ‘Monster Mia,’ Emirati Talent 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of GFF Seasoned Egyptian screenwriter and producer Mariam Naoum sees no shortage of creative talent in Arab television. The harder question is how to give that talent the time, development and routes to market it needs to thrive and build lasting careers. As head of the newly launched CineGouna Series, El Gouna Film Festival ’s first development program dedicated to television, she is trying to tackle some of the obstacles standing in their way. Asked what the industry needs most between time, money and marketing, her answer is clear: “I’ll choose time and marketing.” Related Stories 'Michael Jackson at the Super Bowl' Documentary Coming to Hulu and ESPN The move marks El Gouna’s first formal expansion into series, bringing television into CineGouna, the festival’s industry arm. Its inaugural six-week lab, held ahead of the festival, incubated six projects, with writers developing a series bible and pilot before pitching their work at the festival to broadcasters, producers and directors. Popular on Variety The inaugural cohort comprises “Sent From Above,” by Lebanon’s Dareen Shamseddine, Egyptian projects “Marketing for Beginners,” by Shaimaa Gohar, “To the Edge,” by Mamdouh Salah and Muhammed Abd El-Sattar, “There’s Something Wrong,” by Marim Dagher, and “Half an Hour,” by Mohammed Elsayed Taha, as well as Saudi writer Rana Wael Matar’s “Why, Soad?” For Naoum, series require a different development process from films, from the workflow itself to how projects ultimately reach buyers. Streaming has opened new opportunities for Arab television, but she sees too few buyers for the projects being developed. “You have, in the Arab world, maybe three or four platforms. They cannot cater to the whole market, so you have more projects than they can afford to buy,” she observes. “Maybe the thing that we need to work on is to open more markets outside the region, for either those of Arab origins, like the diaspora, or maybe follow the example of Turkey and Latin America, and the way they manage to sell their projects outside.” “So I think this is the time to start this, because we’re suffocating inside.” Author, screenwriter and producer Haitham Dabbour (“ The Tale of Daye’s Family ”), founder of Irth, a regional content development platform and collaborative writers’ room, shares that concern, arguing that fewer owners means less competition and less room to take risks. “The fewer the platforms, the more cautious they tend to be, and the more they rely on safe, proven formulas,” Dabbour contends. “As a result, the ability to develop and launch truly different kinds of projects becomes much more difficult.” He also points to piracy and rights protection as barriers to expanding the market. “The number of platforms will remain limited as long as we do not combat piracy and protect creators’ rights.” Acclaimed Egyptian television and film director Mariam Abou Ouf (”Whose Empire”) shares that unease. “When it comes to the financing and production landscape, I believe we are approaching a deadlock,” she warns. “The increasing monopolization of the industry is creating a difficult environment, one that is neither healthy nor sustainable.” Yet Abou Ouf sees streaming itself as transformative. “For the first time, a television series has a life that extends far beyond its original broadcast,” she notes. “Audiences can discover it years later, revisit it, and watch it again and again.” More broadly, Naoum has seen Arab television open up to a wider range of storytelling. “When I started, we didn’t have horror, we didn’t have a lot of psychodrama, we didn’t have a lot of crime,” she points out. “Now we have more, so it’s changing.” That creative range was only one consideration in selecting projects for CineGouna Series. “We were looking for projects that are producible, so it wasn’t only a creative approach,” Naoum explains. Before making the selections, she consulted platforms about what they were looking for and took those needs into account alongside the creative merits of each project. Once selected, the writers worked with mentors during the six-week lab to develop their projects. “The lab wasn’t for established writers,” Naoum stresses. “It was mainly for young writers who need the networking and this kind of bridging to the industry.” That connection to the wider industry is central to the program. “I tried to cater projects for the platforms, so that they can find good projects that were incubated in this lab, so they have the trust that our lab worked on this,” she continues. “It’s like shortening the process for the platforms to hunt for projects. We become the ‘middle man’ in that sense.” The question of how those projects might eventually travel beyond the region presents another challenge. Naoum argues that culturally rooted stories can travel if they are well executed. “Our problem in traveling, I don’t think it’s either quality or subject,” she stresses. “We still don’t have the know-how of distribution for series. So it’s more a question of marketing than the creative side.” For CineGouna Series, the first test will be whether the six projects make it beyond the lab. “For me, success is that one or more of the projects can be bought by broadcasters or producers,” Naoum concludes. “To find the way for it to be executed from development to broadcast.” Matthew Rhys Makes Emmy History as First Person to Win Two Lead Acting Emmys in One Night and First Man to Win All Three Top Acting Prizes Never Mind the IP, Here’s How Original Ideas Dominated This Year’s Emmy Races Emmys 2026 Party Guide With Katherine LaNasa, Quinta Brunson and Richard Gadd Rob Reiner Wins Posthumous Emmy for ‘The Bear’ Hiro Murai Becomes First Asian Director to Win Emmy for Comedy Directing With ‘Widow’s Bay’ Seven Variety Cover Stars Win 2026 Emmys Loading comments...

title: A Search for His Biological Father Led to a Top Podcast — and an Endorsement From Ira Glass
full_text: × Skip to main content By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All October 22, 2026 6:31am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sayre Quevedo, host, writer and producer of 'Reaching Out.' Kunjo KR As Sayre Quevedo’s latest podcast premiered, he got a ringing endorsement from Ira Glass, who played some of the show on This American Life and said Quevedo had “invented something completely new.” The podcast, entitled Reaching Out, starts with the premise of Quevedo and his twin brother trying to track down their biological father, whom they had never met and had little information on. This search is interwoven with Quevedo’s diary-like commentary about how he’s feeling about finding his father as well as his own life as he is about to turn 30, and intimate conversations with his brother and mother that delve into how the brothers really feel about each other, and how their paths have diverged. Quevedo is aided in the process by the fact that he has recorded most conversations in his life since his mid-20s, including across the four-year process of finding his birth father. In the end, these conversations, and his own meditations on identity and family, as well as his noted narrative omissions and motives in telling the story, become the main thrust of the podcast. “I don’t know if I’ve heard another podcast that tries to capture a person’s life as completely as this one does, and just what it feels like to be alive right now,” Glass said in describing the show. The six-part series kicked off Sept. 16, from Futuro Studios in partnership with KCRW, and has already won the audio memoir award at the Tribeca Film Festival. The Glass endorsement helped propel the show to the top of Apple Podcast’s series charts that week, with the show still remaining in the top 15. Quevedo, who has previously created podcasts about his family and partners as well as subjects across the world, spoke with The Hollywood Reporter about finding this innovative format, the state of podcasting and how he feels about sharing his life publicly. Why did you start recording your conversations? I have been recording myself consistently. I would say since my mid 20s, but I think the habit probably began when I was a teenager. I think it’s almost a habit at this point. I don’t think about recording or not recording, and a lot of that habit stems from the fact that I grew up without really any documentation of my family. My mom left home when she was very young, and my father obviously was not a part of my life, and so I don’t have really any documents of my family history, and so it just became a way of memorializing, of sort of reminding myself that I exist and that I’m a part of the world and part of history. And in making recordings you’re not necessarily thinking they’ll turn into a podcast or a project? I think, for instance, with searching for my birth father, I’m sure there was some part of my brain that was like, “This is an interesting story. Maybe I’ll turn this into something.” But I think there was another part of my brain that was like, “I would like to remember this. I would like to remember what it felt like to go on this journey. I would like to remember what these conversations sounded like and felt like.” Because I’ve experienced this so often in my life, that I’ve gone through things that I’ve thought, “Oh, I’m never going to forget what it felt like to talk to my father for the first time, or I’m never going to forget how it felt to send that email with my brother,” [reaching out to their father] and then a few months pass or a few years pass, and it’s just a vague notion in my head. And so it does serve that purpose as well as a way to kind of return to these moments. At what point in the process of finding your biological father did you know that this would be a podcast? I think once me and my brother decided to confront my father in person. Because up until that point there was this part of me that, in addition to feeling sort of reticent about looking for him, there was a part of me that felt like it wasn’t going to happen. Though I’m not sure we would have admitted it at the time, I think both of us were so scared of getting that answer and of meeting him that there was some part of me that thought we would never really go through with it. And so after going and confronting him, I was like, something happened. We really did it. And obviously, a lot more happens after that in the series. But I think that was the moment where I was like, I’ve gone through something. I’ve actually done the thing that I was afraid to do. And I think that’s when I knew that there was really a story worth telling, even though I had no idea what was going to happen afterwards. To that point, it seems like the story starts to morph into not just being about your father. When I really began to write the series in earnest, I had this feeling that the search for my father was more of a Trojan horse in some ways. The search for my father was really a way of forcing myself to reflect on my relationship to absence in a lot of ways, and my relationship to desire, and the ways that I had sort of built my life around absences and around yearning and searching for things that I couldn’t have or that were not there. I think that became clear to me as I was listening through all of the conversations that I’d recorded too, not just the conversations but also these minute, quotidian parts of my life. I started to realize I’m doing these same things over and over again. I’m going on these dates and feeling bad about myself. I’m going to the club looking for somebody to go home with. I’m having these conversations with my mother about feeling like I have to to meet this person, and it was through being able to sort of step back and look at the patterns that had sort of cropped up in those recordings, that I was able to see “Oh, I’m actually going through something completely different.” The search for my father is actually helping me see that I was going through something else that I wasn’t able to fully see or recognize in the moment of it. Throughout the podcast, you’re willing to get very personal and be open about yourself, including vulnerable emotional moments as you navigate romantic relationships, as well as others where you acknowledge you’re kind of being a jerk. Were you nervous putting all of that out there? I still feel nervous about it. There’s a lot of me in this work. I mean, it’s personal, obviously, but there’s a lot of me in this work. My philosophy around how I make personal work is that whatever honesty I’m asking of the people that I include in this work, I have to be tenfold more honest because it’s such a big thing to ask, especially my family, my mother and my twin. It’s such a huge thing to ask people to share something so vulnerable with the public, and also to share it with me, and to give me the power to tell that story. And so I’m sharing a lot of parts of myself that frankly, there’s parts of it that I still feel shame about. There’s versions of myself in this story that are extremely judgmental, extremely critical, critical of myself and of others, and parts of myself that are also at odds with how I would like to be in the world or how I’d like to see myself. My hope is that by sharing those parts of myself that are maybe slightly less likable, slightly less relatable, that people can sort of recognize and accept those parts of themselves as well. What did you make of the Ira Glass endorsement, in which he said you’d invented “something completely new,” and are taking the format of his own show and pushing it further? If you say podcasting, that’s the guy people think of, you know, so it was really surreal, and I probably haven’t fully processed what that means. But it was extremely affirming. I’ve worked in audio since I was 15 years old. I’m 33 now, so to receive that kind of feedback from somebody of that stature and who I respect that much really makes it feel worth it to put everything on the line and to make something that where I took some risks both stylistically and personally, to share to share it with the world Were you looking for a new kind of format when you created the show? I try not to repeat myself in terms of the form of the work that I’m making. Maybe this is controversial, but I consider podcasting an art and an art form. I think it’s a documentary form and medium and expression. But there’s also a lot of creativity in the work, and I don’t want to make the same art twice. I want to challenge myself. But I wouldn’t say necessarily the style of the work was done with that in mind as much as in trying to find the right form for it. I wanted to make something that felt reflective of my life in a real way, but that also felt like the kind of art that I enjoy. I wanted to make something literary. I’m a long time reader and grew up reading and love reading and love words as an art form. So I just felt like, at this point, given the state of the industry and the state of where things are at, like why not just take the risk and make something that feels like something I would want to read or something that I would want to watch. Things are so dire in podcasting right now that there’s really nothing to lose in terms of making something that maybe alienates some people because it doesn’t sound like everything that they’ve already heard, and so that was sort of the ethos that I went into making the work. What’s feeling dire for you in the podcasting industry? There has been a little bit less of the resources that so many of us who were in podcasting in the early 2010s and 2020s had. As those resources have gone away, as the Gimlets of the world have gone away, as the Pineapple Streets have gone away, there is a feeling that there’s just a lot less room to make risky creative work that is not meant to engage the broadest possible audience, but is meant for people who just want to listen to something experimental or strange or creative. And so I think that’s the direness, the feeling that there’s less room for this kind of work to exist, and I do hope that the success of the work gives some permission to whoever still has the money and resources to take some risks because people did obviously respond to it in a positive way. But I do think that’s the direness of the moment, alongside the layoffs and everything else. The tightening of the belt also leads to a tightening of what is seen as creatively profitable, or creatively possible or worthy of risk in the moment, and that’s a hard place to be for a lot of my friends and colleagues. title: Italy’s Movie and TV Spending Drops Amid Tax Incentive Uncertainty
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 22, 2026 6:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Rome, Italy. Christopher Furlong/Getty Images Italy’s inward cinema, TV and video-on-demand sectors content investment fell in 2025 for the first time since 2018, the annual APA report released at the MIA Market in Rome indicated. The overall audiovisual content investment dropped 7.4 percent to €2 billion ($2.24 billion) last year, compared with the 2024 stats, according to the APA, the Italian audiovisual producers association. The dropoff came amid a government overhaul of Italy’s tax credit system for indie producers and local audiences shifting from traditional linear TV broadcasters to emerging streaming platforms. The latest APA report also comes against the background of an Italian industry dealing with screens of all sizes and new value placed on original IP as storytellers find new platforms to reach audiences. According to the APA report, Italian scripted productions for TV and VOD platforms saw their inward investment fall to €122 million ($137 million), while fiction production dropped to €740 million ($830 million) last year. “The main factor affecting the sector’s resilience is uncertainty surrounding the public funding framework, from the amount of available resources to eligibility criteria and application timelines. This situation hampers producers’ ability to plan ahead, increases financing costs and reduces margins, placing pressure on all companies, particularly smaller businesses, with consequences for liquidity and investment capacity,” the APA report indicated with commentary. As elsewhere in the global industry the market share of Italian linear free and pay TV channel continues to fall as streaming platform grew to a 43 percent share in 2025. “In the short to medium term, it is expected to surpass linear television in value,” the APA report warned about the continuing dominance of streaming platforms in Italy. European producers at the MIA Market this week heard they no longer compete just with each other but against American studios and streamers, YouTube and social platforms. So they require new public and private financing to maintain their audience share and international revenues. THR

title: Yes, ‘Heated Rivalry’ Is Really Headed to Movie Theaters
full_text: × Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All October 22, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie in 'Heated Rivalry.' Sabrina Lantos/HBO Have you been hoping to see Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov on the big screen? You’re in luck — Heated Rivalry , the hit Canadian hockey romance series, is officially heading to theaters for limited engagement marathon screenings, distributor Sphere Abacus announced Thursday morning. The Crave original series, which airs on HBO Max in the U.S., is celebrating its one-year anniversary a little early, with screenings of all six episodes of the first season kicking off on Nov. 6. Sphere Abacus, the Bell Media company that helped bring the show international, partnered with Regal Cinemas in the U.S. for the release. Thursday’s announcement comes after speculation on social media throughout the week. Related Stories Lifestyle 'Heated Rivalry' Goes All In on Physical Media Including Special Edition Blu-Ray and DVD TV 'Yaga' Review: Carrie-Anne Moss and Hudson Williams in AMC+'s Intriguing but Undercooked Brew of Modern Crime and Ancient Folklore From Nov. 6 through Nov. 30, fans of the show can revisit the series across three paired episode screenings: episodes one and two (“Rookies” and “Olympians”), episodes three and four (“Hunter” and “Rose”) and episodes five and six (“I’ll Believe in Anything” and “The Cottage”). Tickets will run at $9.99 per screening. Regal will show the episodes in over 275 of its own locations in the U.S. The company also serves as the nationwide distributor, bringing the show to 650 theaters including AMC and Cinemark. Regal showings will include welcome content from the cast and director, show creator Jacob Tierney . Participating locations will offer themed, limited-time cocktails: Summer in Montreal and Russians Don’t Blush. “ Heated Rivalry is a global phenomenon creating a rush of social media and press activity wherever it lands. We’re very excited to give audiences the opportunity to watch the drama unfold on big screens in North America, the UK, Australia & New Zealand,” Sphere Abacus’ executive director of global distribution and partnerships Hana Palmer said in a release. Based on Rachel Reid’s novel of the same name, Heated Rivalry focuses on the complicated situationship between Shane Hollander, played by Hudson Williams , and Ilya Rozanov, played by Connor Storrie . The pair are generational talents in the world of professional hockey and sworn on-ice rivals, who meet as teenagers. The first novel of Reid’s book series, Game Changers , which the novel Heated Rivalry hails from, centered on François Arnaud’s character Scott Hunter and Robbie G.K. ’s character Kip Grady; it served as secondary material for the first season. The show’s season one cast was rounded out by Christina Chang, Dylan Walsh, Sophie Nélisse and Ksenia Daniela Kharlamova. Season two of the series is filming in Toronto, and features a slew of new cast members. Williams and Storrie return to front the series, with Justice Smith, Charlie Gillespie, Daniel Diemer and Shaheen Jafargholi joining them in leading roles for the second season. Tickets for Heated Rivalry ‘s theatrical event are available at the box office and Regal’s website and mobile app. THR

title: Space 11 & SK Films Bringing Artemis II To The Big Screen With ‘Return To The Moon: The Story Of Artemis II’
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Space 11 & SK Films Bringing Artemis II To The Big Screen With ‘Return To The Moon: The Story Of Artemis II’ Neon Joins Yuval Abraham & Rachel Szor’s Explosive Gaza-Israel Doc ‘NAZA’ ‘Dune: Part Three’ Smashes BFI Imax Record With 33,000 Admissions Sold In First 24 Hours View All October 22, 2026 5:58am Add us as a Google Preferred Source NASA's Artemis II Space Launch System rocket carrying the Orion spacecraft lifts off from Launch Complex 39B at Kennedy Space Center. Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images EXCLUSIVE : Space 11 Corp. and SK Films are behind Return to the Moon: The Story of Artemis II , a new space film with Duncan Copp and Christopher Riley directing. The producers are targeting a PLF rollout for the film, which they say will combine NASA’s real Artemis II mission imagery with the voices of the four astronauts who lived it. Worldwide theatrical release is targeted for summer 2027. The synopsis reads: “Between April 1 and 11, 2026, the crew of the spacecraft Integrity traveled 695,081 miles and reached 252,756 miles from Earth, setting a new record for human spaceflight. The film follows the mission from the launch pad to splashdown in the Pacific.” Related Stories News 'CBS Mornings' To Hold Town Hall With Artemis Mission Astronauts News Artemis II Crew Successfully Splashes Down Off San Diego Coast Space 11 says it is collaborating with NASA under a Space Act Agreement to shoot giant-screen interviews with the Artemis II crew: Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover, Mission Specialist Christina Koch and Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency. Watch on Deadline The narrative will be interwoven by the four astronauts in their own words and NASA’s high-resolution photography and footage, reformatted for giant screens. A 45 minute version and a shorter format are being planned to go out via SK’s network of giant-screen and specialty theaters, including IMAX theaters, museums, science-centers, and other institutional venues. The film will also be offered to school groups. Duncan Copp and Christopher Riley have both worked with NASA’s astronauts, engineers and scientists, past and present. Copp and Riley produced Ron Howard-presented In the Shadow of the Moon , winner of the World Cinema Documentary Audience Award at Sundance. Riley, a two-time BAFTA nominee, has worked with the Artemis II crew before, on hit immersive experience The Moonwalkers: A Journey with Tom Hanks , which he co-wrote with Hanks. The film is produced by Andrea Iervolino ( Ferrari ), founder of Space 11. Producer Nicola Allieta will also participate in this production. SK, the natural history and science content specialist, most recently released Ocean Dreams , narrated by Shailene Woodley. Andrea Iervolino, Founder of Space 11, stated: “Artemis II belongs to everyone who looked up at the Moon in April. We are honored to tell this story in collaboration with NASA and alongside the four astronauts who took us there. Our responsibility is to make a film that everyone behind this mission, from the teams at NASA and the Canadian Space Agency to the families who waited at home, will watch with pride. With Duncan Copp and Christopher Riley, who know this crew and this history as few filmmakers do, and with SK Films, we will share that journey with audiences around the world.” Bert Ulrich, Executive Vice President of Production at Space 11 and former NASA Film and Television Liaison, added: “In more than two decades at NASA, I learned that nothing moves people like real imagery and the voices of those who were actually there. This film is built on both: NASA’s own photography and footage, and the Artemis II crew recounting the flight themselves. On a giant screen, it is as close as most of us will ever come to flying aboard Integrity. If it inspires young people to reach for a seat on a future mission, it will have done what the best space documentaries have always done.” “NASA’s Artemis II Mission is the perfect subject for giant screen cinema: it invites audiences to experience a historic accomplishment, with the extraordinarily personal perspective of its astronauts, on a scale unparalleled by any other cinematic experience” said Wendy MacKeigan, CEO of SK Films. “We are excited to be working with Space 11 and the brilliant creative team to bring this film to audiences around the world.” Skydance Nordics & Germany Boss Spotlights Her Approach Town Hall Takeaways; Are Stock Jitters Valid Or A Market Overreaction? title: Rupert Grint Sets Next Project: Noiser Audiobook Adaptation of ‘Treasure Island’ (Exclusive)

In an adaptation for podcast network Noiser, Grint is set to play every single character from Robert Louis Stevenson’s classic 1883 novel, including the wide-eyed Jim Hawkins, silver-tongued Long John Silver, the rum-soaked Billy Bones and half-mad castaway Ben Gunn. Episodes will drop weekly starting Dec. 8. “Noiser’s serialised audiobooks now reach over 50 million listens a year, which shows how much appetite there is for great storytelling in this format,” Noiser CEO Pascal Hughes told The Hollywood Reporter . “ Treasure Island is where we bring the whole family in. Our hope is that kids fall in love with classic storytelling and grown-ups rediscover it.” Related Stories Business Italy's Movie and TV Spending Drops Amid Tax Incentive Uncertainty Movies Stephen Lang, Uli Edel Reunite on 'Mercy Rider' 30 Years After 'Last Exit to Brooklyn' (Exclusive) Stevenson’s 1883 novel gave the world much of what we now think of as pirate lore — the treasure map marked with an X, the squawking parrot and a deserted island hiding a fortune. When a weathered old sailor arrives at a remote West Country tavern, young Jim Hawkins is swept into the adventure of a lifetime. A treasure map hidden in an old buccaneer’s sea chest takes him from the fog-laden English coast to the sun-scorched shores of a perilous island aboard the Hispaniola. But the crew harbors a dangerous secret, and Long John Silver is not all he seems. Grint is known around the world for his role as Ron Weasley in the film adaptations of Harry Potter and is set to reprise the role from February to May in Broadway’s Harry Potter and the Cursed Child . He has been filling in for Romo, who in September pleaded no contest to a charge of operating while intoxicated stemming from an incident that took place in Milwaukee in July . At the time, Romo said he hoped to return. He did not. CBS Sports and the former quarterback said earlier this month that they would split , a move sports-media aficionados attributed to some disillusionment with Romo’s recent on-air performance. Watt also has critical on-the-field experience, having played for the Houston Texans and Arizona Cardinals. He is the only player in NFL history to record multiple seasons with at least 20 sacks. TV-sports outlets have been pouring out money to lure top NFL announcers , with Fox and Disney shelling out top dollar to lure, respectively, Tom Brady and Troy Aikman and Joe Buck. Many top announcers’ contracts are expected to lapse after the end of this season, including not only Aikman’s, but Greg Olsen’s at Fox, and Al Michaels’ at Amazon. ESPN has secured Buck to a new deal — but so far, not Aikman — and Amazon has signed Kirk Herbstreit, who also calls college game at ESPN, to provisional terms. ESPN and Amazon have so far declined to comment on the status of those announcers’ deals. TV networks rushed to line up top talent to call games after the NFL struck a pivotal 11-year rights deal in 2021 . At the time, the thought from many TV sports chiefs was that they had to spend money to make money. Romo carved out new terrain at CBS Sports after revealing a knack for predicting game play — all but forcing CBS to re-sign the former Dallas Cowboys quarterback to a multi-season pact in 2020 valued at around $17 million a year. Since that time, most of CBS’ contemporaries have followed suit. When ESPN signed former Fox Sports mainstays Buck and Aikman to deals in 2022 to call “Monday Night Football, ” it was seen as a critical move that would help the Disney-backed sports-media giant soothe what had become a troubled relationship with the NFL. Amazon lured NBC Sports’ Al Michaels and ESPN’s Herbstreit to serve as the voices for “Thursday Night Football.” And Fox secured the services of none other than Brady , a move that crowded out sportscaster Olsen. People familiar with the market estimate top football-booth personnel can earn between $15 million and $20 million per season. CBS Sports may have other talent issues to juggle in weeks to come. Ian Eagle, a veteran who calls secondary NFL games for CBS Sports, is also believed to have a contract that is set to lapse. title: Peacock’s Hot Streak: Two Quarters of Profit After Years Of Losses
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 22, 2026 4:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Comcast president Mike Cavanagh Kevork Djansezian/Getty Images Peacock , the marquee NBCUniversal streamer, on Thursday delivered its second consecutive profitable quarter on the back of 48 million subscribers, up from 41 million in the year-earlier period but flat quarter-to-quarter. As Comcast, led by Brian Roberts and Michael Cavanagh, reported its third-quarter financials, Peacock posted a pre-tax profit of $261 million, which followed a $189 million profit in the most recent second quarter and a $217 million year-ago loss. Peacock’s maiden second-quarter profit was lifted by FIFA World Cup games, which contributed $440 million in incremental media revenues. The third quarter included $224 million of incremental advertising revenue from the FIFA World Cup as the final games were shown at the start of the latest financial quarter on Peacock and NBCUniversal’s Spanish language Telemundo service. Comcast’s content and experiences businesses reported revenue of $10.5 billion, up 6.5 percent from a year ago, and adjusted EBITIDA up 29 percent to $1.8 billion. Media revenue rose 13 percent to $5.35 billion, with adjusted EBITDA of $769 million. Studios revenue fell 1.1 percent to $2.96 billion, with adjusted EBITDA of $402 million. The latest quarter saw contributions to Universal from Christopher Nolan’s epic The Odyssey , Minions & Monsters and the breakout horror pic Obsession for Focus Features. Peacock, the streaming service of Comcast’s entertainment unit NBCUniversal, saw revenue come to $1.8 billion in the most recent quarter, up from $1.4 billion of revenue in the prior-year period after recent subscription price increases and lower programming costs. As Comcast continues to face a broadband division downturn, the media conglomerate posted third-quarter revenue down 6 percent to $29.29 billion, compared with $31.19 billion in the year-earlier period. Net income attributable to Comcast rose 3.5 percent to $3.44 billion, against $3.33 billion in the same period of 2025. Comcast did manage to trim its broadband losses to 376,000 subscribers during the third quarter, an improvement from 475,000 broadband customer losses a year-ago. The latest results from Comcast follows a separation from Versant, the cable TV-focused spinoff from NBCUniversal that runs CNBC, MS NOW, USA, Golf Channel and other assets. On a morning analyst call, Cavanagh said the Versant separation transaction would be completed by the middle of 2027, and “we’re well into the execution phase,” including building out standalone companies. “While there is still significant work ahead, we have a clear path to completion and remain focused on creating two companies with the strategic flexibility, financial strength and leadership to compete and grow independently,” he added. Cavanagh also welcomed so far holding Peacock’s subscriber base at around 48 million over the last two quarters amid rate increases. As to future profits or losses for the the streaming platform, he added: “The quarters ahead can get lumpy, depending on when rates kick in for different properties.” To continue growing Peacock, NBCUniversal will be bundling the streamer with rival platforms, as with a recently announced multiyear deal between NBCUniversal and YouTube to bring Peacock to YouTube premium subscribers. “We are interested in doing this with others as well. Different bundles will be different for different types of partners, but we’re looking to make them additive to the business,” Cavanagh told analysts. CFO Jason Armstrong also warned Comcast would take a “significant” restructuring charge at over $1 billion in the fourth quarter as the media conglomerate continues to refocus its mobile business around convergent cable and Internet products to fend off competition in broadband from wireless providers like Verizon and T-Mobile. Brian L. full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All October 22, 2026 3:54am Add us as a Google Preferred Source (R to L): Jack Hudson, Stephen Lang, Uli Edel Avatar star Stephen Lang is reuniting with director Uli Edel 37 years after Lang’s breakthrough performance in Edel’s Last Exit to Brooklyn . Lang, who plays Colonel Miles Quaritch in James Cameron’s Avatar franchise, has signed on to star in The Mercy Rider , a modern-day Western thriller which Edel will direct from a script by Richard Julian. Lang plays Joe McCabe, a former soldier and reclusive Texas rancher who decides to risk everything to fight back against immigration authorities after they detain a hardworking local father. Determined to reunite the farmer with his family, McCabe comes up against a hard-line immigration agent, Harvey “Hawk” Walters, played by Irish actor Jack Hudson . The film is set to shoot in Mexico. Mac Brown, a line producer on Last Exit , and an executive producer on Martin Scorsese’s Oscar-winning The Departed , and Neil Burger’s 2017 hit The Upside , will produce The Mercy Rider with Hudson. German-born Edel made his feature debut with the sleeper hit Christiane F. (1981), the story of a young Berlin heroin addict. Last Exit to Brooklyn (1989) was his English-language debut. The adaptation of Hubert Selby Jr.’s novel, set in the working-class underbelly of Red Hook on the Brooklyn waterfront, circa 1952, starred Lang as a shop steward who is a closeted homosexual, and Jennifer Jason Leigh as a prostitute secretly searching for love. While just a modest commercial success, Last Exit proved a breakout film for all involved. Edel would go on to direct the Oscar-nominated The Baader Meinhof Complex (2008). Lang is represented by Innovative Artists. Hudson is represented by International Artists Management and Framework Entertainment. Edel is represented by Gersh. THR
